editorials.title: Forging consensus: On India and the SCO meeting
editorials.passage:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s attendance at the annual meeting of Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) leaders in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, marking 25 years of the Eurasian grouping, had a multi-pronged agenda. This was an occasion to meet his counterparts, for the first time since the U.S.-Israel war on Iran began more than six months ago, which has inflicted economic costs on the whole grouping. The grouping includes Iran, as well as Pakistan that has emerged a mediator between Iran and the U.S., and the Bishkek declaration that condemned the U.S. and Israel’s attacks on Iran and supported Iran’s right to peaceful nuclear technology under the NPT, was significant. Many of the SCO members are also in the BRICS grouping who Mr. Modi will host in Delhi on September 12-13 — this includes Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. New Delhi is keen to forge consensus on a joint declaration, which has been difficult due to UAE-Iran tensions and Mr. Modi’s discussions with Mr. Pezeshkian included BRICS cooperation. India’s ties with the Central Asian Republics have flagged due to other preoccupations, making Mr. Modi’s visits to Tashkent and Bishkek, and meetings with regional leaders this time, an important initiative to revive talks on trade, critical minerals, tourism and other areas. As Pakistan takes over the SCO chairmanship, the Bishkek Summit allowed Mr. Modi to set out India’s agenda for the coming year. His speech at the Summit focused on the importance of dismantling the ecosystem of “terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens”, calling on the SCO to eschew “double standards” on terrorism. He also pressed for a strong message to countries that “use terrorism as an instrument of policy and provide safe haven and support to terrorists” — a pointed reference to India’s oft-repeated concerns about Pakistan. The Bishkek declaration’s inclusion of strong language on “all forms” of terrorism, including cross-border, has thus been welcomed by New Delhi. It remains to be seen how far the Pakistan presidency will take these ideas forward.

Compared to the high-octane optics and the Modi-Putin-Xi handshake at the 2025 Tianjin SCO Summit, this year’s summit was relatively sombre. The U.S.’s tariffs, its war with Iran and sanctions on Russia have damaged economic security, energy security and connectivity (the Hormuz Strait blockade), and pose major challenges to the grouping. For India, after tensions with Pakistan had peaked last year after the Pahalgam attacks and the four-day conflict, the past year has been sobering, given Pakistan’s diplomatic forays with the U.S., and the new security pact with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. In the altered geopolitical framing, India must seek to broaden its engagement with all regional multilateral organisations such as the SCO.

editorials.title: Welcome move: On the Supreme Court and Gen Z protesters
editorials.passage:
In what should be termed a salutary gesture, the Supreme Court of India, at the request of the Union government, invoked its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash criminal cases against the youth who had taken part in nationwide protests seeking examination reforms and government accountability. Led by a group, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), in response to Chief Justice of India’s “unemployment” and “cockroaches” remark — these protests swelled in numbers and reach, forcing the then Union Minister of Education, Dharmendra Pradhan, to resign. Among the demands for halting the agitations was the CJP’s call to withdraw the FIRs against protesters in Delhi and other States/Union Territories, which the Court has granted, while directing the Centre to ensure that no fresh FIRs are registered over the protests in July. That the Centre asked for this step by the Court shows how the CJP’s agitations resonated with the youth of the country, who agreed with the movement’s core demands. It is also an acknowledgment by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government that this is a pressing issue that revealed its failings, particularly the series of paper leaks across India over the years, compounded by an employment deficit for youth.

The Centre’s stand in the CJP matter is in stark contrast to how it has dealt with dissent on other issues that have driven thousands to protest in recent years. The most prominent among these were the farmer-led protests in and around Delhi, and the agitations against the communally motivated Citizenship (Amendment) Act. Both were largely peaceful, but this did not prevent the government from foisting serious charges including those related to terrorism and sedition, on peaceful protesters, many of whom remain in jail without trial or bail. Legitimate protest has long been a means of defusing pent-up discontent with government policies in India. The Centre has instead sought to criminalise it, branding dissent and disaffection as sedition to create a chilling effect. The CJP managed to overcome that ploy not only through the justness of its demands but also because the protesters’ identities as youth and students transcended the limited categories of religion, caste and even class (“richer farmers”) that the BJP sought to use to sow discord and delegitimise them. Even if it is too much to expect the Centre to seek similar relief for those held in earlier cases, the Court would do well to apply to them the standard it has now set for the CJP. Until it does, the relief granted to the CJP and its sympathisers will remain an exception rather than a principle.

editorials.title: Court verdicts raise serious question on coercive use of law
editorials.passage: Two recent judicial interventions should concern anyone who believes that the State must be firm in dealing with disorder but equally careful in dealing with dissent. The Allahabad High Court’s decision to cancel the detention of student and activist Aakriti Chaudhary under the National Security Act raises questions about how the police built their case. Chaudhary was accused of instigating stone-pelting and arson during the Noida workers’ protest this April, but the State could not immediately produce the video it claimed established her role. The court also pointed out several procedural lapses in the sequence of her arrest and the manner of issuing notices. It described the State’s version as a “concocted story” and even ordered compensation.Similar concerns are reflected on a wider scale in the Supreme Court’s intervention in the cases arising from student protests during July 20-25. It ordered the closure of FIRs connected to the protests lodged around the country and barred fresh cases from being opened. At the same time, it allowed proceedings against those identified as having serious criminal antecedents. That distinction is important. The court did not say that students are immune from criminal law. It held that bona fide participation in a protest cannot by itself justify treating a young person as accused and putting their future at risk..The police response, however, needs closer examination. A protest can turn violent, and those responsible must be investigated and prosecuted. But being at a protest does not make a person responsible for the violence. The police have to show what the individual accused actually did; a mere allegation cannot stand for proof.The Allahabad judgement also draws attention to the way the detention was carried out. The safeguards laid down by law cannot be treated as formalities, especially when the State applies a law as stringent as the NSA. The case raises a fundamental question: did the circumstances warrant the use of a law that permits preventive detention? The manner in which it was invoked makes the question difficult to avoid.The larger issue is whether the State is exercising its coercive powers with the restraint and legal discipline that democracy requires. editorials.title: Lesson for India to act fast on scientific data
editorials.passage: Last week’s flash floods, which devastated vast swathes stretching south from the Nepal-Tibet border, have killed more than a thousand people even as thousands of others remain untraced. Two-thirds of a glacier on the Langtang Lirung peak near the border broke off, sending debris plunging vertically into the Lhende stream and causing a colossal wall of water, mud, ice and rocks that ripped through a 90-km stretch down the corridor of Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers within an hour or so. Entire settlements along the way were wiped out.The disaster is a painful lesson on the importance of preparing for catastrophes of such ferocity with the tools in hand. Among other things, a failure to act in time on information from space-based monitoring led to such a massive toll in life, property and ecology.A fleet of sophisticated ground-observing satellites—including the Nasa-Isro Synthetic Aperture Radar or NISAR and the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-1 constellation—are constantly patrolling along a low-Earth orbit to detect tell-tale early signs of such calamities. NISAR and Sentinel-1, which is run under the European Union’s Copernicus programme for environmental observation, are polar-orbiting, radar-imagery satellites that use synthetic apertures to detect even changes of millimetres on the ground. They relay the data to stations located across the world, particularly for tracking crust deformations, floods, volcanic activities and earthquakes. These satellites can detect small changes on the Earth’s surface even in mountainous regions like the Himalayas..A recent analysis of data relayed by Sentinel-1, published in Nature, showed that the Langtang Lirung peak glacier was accelerating while moving downhill; the latest observation was taken just seven days before the disaster struck. China’s Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, Switzerland’s Asian Mountain Academic Alliance and the US’s Stimson Centre had analysed satellite images to find changes in the glacier and the surrounding terrain that suggested that the system was becoming unstable. And yet, no alarm was sounded—let alone evacuation carried out—to save people in the path of the catastrophe.While this is a lesson for the world, India in particular needs to sit up and take note considering lakhs of people in the fragile Lower Himalayas and Indo-Gangetic plains face similar threats, and the impact of such destruction could be manifold larger..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Sic transit Gloria
editorials.passage: The trouble with putting people on a pedestal is that their follies tend to get magnified. So it was with Gloria Steinem, the groundbreaking feminist activist whose death at 92 was announced Thursday. But even those who find her work for the CIA projecting American ideas during the Cold War problematic cannot begrudge her formidable work for women’s causes. Her activism, from undercover reporting as a Playboy Bunny to championing laws against discrimination and sexual violence, inspired women around the world. She admittedly learnt about grassroots activism during the years she spent in India in the late 1950s on a fellowship, when she saw Vinoba Bhave’s Bhoodan movement up close. On her passing, the world would do well to reassess what it still needs to do to bridge the gender gap..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Rule of three
editorials.passage:
Whether primitive or sophisticated, the human brain has the ability to effortlessly grasp the presence of up to three objects within one’s visual field without actually having to count. The higher threshold is four objects; but three is the minimum universal ability. Therefore, in all pre-rational philosophy and symbolism, the number, three, has a centrality. The idea of trigunas ( sattva , rajas , tamas ) in the Samhkya or the Trinity in several spiritual traditions has its origin in this innate capacity of the brain. Since the action involved is entirely prescient, irrational practices such as magic and witchcraft also rely heavily on the use of three. The best literary example is Shakespeare’s famous witches in Macbeth . They are three in number; for completing the spell they plan to cast on Macbeth, each takes three steps, making them nine steps in a complete circle: “Thrice to thine, thrice to mine, and thrice again ...”

Cultural Anthropology explains witchcraft not as mere superstition but as a logical and functional system designed to cope with catastrophic disasters. In his landmark work, Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande , the anthropologist, E.E. Evans-Pritchard, argued that witchcraft and magic are attempts to plug the gaps in perception that science cannot explain.

The Lok Sabha secretariat does not accept the terms, magic and witchcraft. The nation learnt this when Rahul Gandhi’s use of the term, ‘magician’, during the delimitation debate in April was promptly expunged. Yet, the ‘thrice to thine, thrice to mine, and thrice again’ pattern of policy-dance is very much in the public eye. The three triads are: one, Constitutional Amendment-Census-Delimitation; two, Communalism-Census- ghar wapsi ; and, three, SIR-Census-Demography. In all three, the census is the linchpin; and the three are organically connected to an irrational ideological fantasy .

The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill brought to the Lok Sabha was, in the first place, completely unnecessary. If the government had not tied up — again, entirely unnecessarily — the Women’s Reservation Bill to the Census after 2026, the Bill could have been implemented. If the proposed amendment was just about delinking the 2026 Census from the reservation, it would have easily been adopted. But the goal was to hasten the setting up of the Delimitation Commission and, in turn, to alter the country’s political landscape. The Constitution Amendment Bill was entirely unnecessary as the 2002 Amendment Act related to delimitation already provides for the setting up of a Delimitation Commission for “a census after 2026”. That particular census ‘after 2026’ is already announced and half way through its course. However, the government may not get the required time-window for a fundamental restricting of Parliament and assembly constituencies before the 2029 elections if it were to wait for the final census data to be published, as required by the Delimitation Act. Therefore, the vastly irrational Amendment Bill was hurriedly brought in. Defeated, it now lies in the annals of the Lok Sabha proceedings.

The second triad of Communalism-Census- ghar wapsi was born out of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s theory of Indian population. It has been a central part of the narrative of the RSS-VHP — that a time will come when Muslim and Christian populations in India will overwhelm the Hindu population. The theory is so utterly baseless and ridiculous that it does not deserve even a refutation. If this did not happen in the past during the centuries when large parts of South Asia were dominated by medieval Islamic rulers with regard to Muslim population, and during the colonial times with regard to Christian population, can it happen now when more than four-fifths of India’s population is Hindu? Yet, the irrepressible desire to avenge the past seems to have been embedded in the design of the census. It has, for the first time, asked a strange question: it seeks to find out names of spouses. When the data are collected, the census will have a complete list of couples who have entered into the inter-religious wedlock. Can anyone guarantee that the data will not fall in the hands of those RSS-VHP front-liners who are euphemistically described as the ‘fringe elements’? In the past, the census was used for planning and increasing citizens’ access to welfare. Never was it interested in finding out who married whom, and how to accelerate ‘ghar wapsi’.

The third triad is the SIR-Census-Demography. The timing of the creation of the High-Level Committee on Demographic Changes passes no rational scrutiny. The census exercise is on and will gather data on population, migration, religions and languages. The massive SIR has already mapped ‘outsiders’. Where is the need to undertake an overlapping exercise? Does the HLCDC have in its armoury an exclusionary method deadlier than the SIR? Sadly, all that the demography study is likely to achieve is reducing the credibility of the Indian census. Perhaps the Committee may succeed in intensifying the fear of massive infiltration which the BJP-RSS has been spreading for decades as a social theory without any significant evidence on the ground.

The three triads appear to have been set up towards fulfilling a sociological fantasy embedded in the history of the RSS. During the 1920s, V.D. Savarkar produced his thesis on Hindutva, The Essentials of Hindutva , and B.S. Moonje initiated K.B. Hedgewar into establishing a sangh , the RSS. Racism was a common theme in European politics in that decade. Those ideas of racial superiority, of religious and ethnic groups to be conceptualised differently into ‘loyal citizens’ and ‘suspect citizens’, found place in their political playbooks. Savarkar positioned a conflation of pitru bhumi (fatherland) together with punya bhumi (the land of origin of scriptures) as the defining test of citizen’s loyalty to the nation.

The three triads of policy imposition by the current regime are guided by that deeply flawed conceptualisation of India as a nation. If these threesome policies were to succeed, India will never be the same again — socially, culturally and politically. On the other hand, even if they fail, as most likely they will, the standing of institutions like the Election Commission of India, the census, and the associated processes will have sunk lower and shrunk further. But perhaps the policies are, as cultural anthropology thinks, an attempt to cope with the other challenges arising out of a devastated economy and a degenerated education system — a kind of a political witchcraft. But the impact of these policy-decisions on India may continue to haunt the country long after the third term of the government comes to an end.

G.N. Devy is author of Citizen Under Siege

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Treating domestic work as formal job could be the secret to successful marriage
editorials.passage:
Sir — What is the secret to a successful marriage? A man recently shared his take on this on Reddit. He said that a husband should give the wife a fixed monthly amount for all the work she does at home, money which will be hers to spend as she sees fit. Such an arrangement challenges conventional Indian household dynamics by treating domestic work as a formal job. More couples could consider such a marital payroll model. Yet, money cannot be a substitute for respect — after all, employees in the office are not disrespected just because they draw a salary. More important, paying the woman for domestic labour should not be an excuse to not lend her a helping hand.

Sir — The Himalayas bring to mind snow-covered peaks, deep valleys, and swift-flowing rivers. Yet, beyond this beauty lies a highly unstable and continuously evolving geological region (“Nature’s fury”, Sept 2). The Himalayas are among the youngest mountain ranges on Earth, and their formation is still ongoing. This is why the region is prone to frequent earthquakes, landslides, avalanches, cloudbursts, flash floods and disasters associated with glaciers. Uncontrolled construction in natural river corridors must be restricted. Himalayan countries should establish mechanisms for rapid sharing of information on climate.

Dattaprasad Shirodkar, Mumbai

Sir — The floods in Nepal are yet another warning that the Himalayas can no longer be treated as an ordinary frontier for development. Glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region are melting rapidly, and the rivers they feed sustain millions of people. For India and China, this demands a radically different diplomatic imagination. The two powers should consider a Himalayan framework treaty with the region’s other countries, including a moratorium on industrial mining and large hydropower projects in the most fragile landscapes.

Himangka Kaushik, New Delhi

Sir — The prime minister of Nepal, Balendra Shah, is facing the enormous task of rebuilding communities and critical infrastructure following last week’s deadly flash floods (“Nepal new leaders’ herculean task”, Sept 1). The 36-year-old prime minister and his largely inexperienced cabinet are confronting their first major national crisis that is also shaping up to be the country’s worst disaster in a decade.

Sir — As India mourns those affected by the devastating floods in Nepal, questions arise over the decision of Prime Minister Narendra Modi to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit rather than remain in India to oversee disaster response. Even though specialised institutions and modern communications ensure relief operations continue effectively regardless of a leader’s physical location, visible empathy from the leadership remains important.

Sir — The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal are a serious wake-up call for humanity. Climate change and deforestation will continue to cause such events with increasing intensity unless immediate steps are taken to prevent environmental degradation. Global sea levels are rising due to the melting of glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland and the Arctic. This is an irreversible change that could cause irreparable damage.

Sir — Rescuers reached flood-affected areas in Nepal and carried out their life-saving efforts in record time. Nepal’s rescue teams remain on permanent standby due to the country’s volatile geography. The United Nations must extend its full support and accelerate ongoing rescue operations to reach missing and trapped survivors as quickly as possible.

Sir — The recurring onion price swings expose deep structural weaknesses in agricultural markets. During periods of glut, farmers are forced to sell at distress prices and during shortages, consumers bear the burden of inflation. The Centre recently released buffer stock, made retail interventions, and decided to avoid export bans. This is a calibrated approach.

Sir — The rising prices of essential commodities are placing ordinary people in financial stress. To check pre-Puja inflation, the Bengal government should introduce fair price shops or authorised doorstep distribution networks. This would protect consumers from unscrupulous traders.

D. Bhattacharyya, Calcutta

Sir — A book must be understood in the context of its time and social milieu. The Manusmriti is a part of the dharmashastras (“Code of conduct”, Aug 28). In today’s context, however, invoking the Manusmriti to determine rules of conduct may not be valid since several of its prescriptions justify the subjugation of women and the lower castes. Such ideas need to be challenged.

Nibedita Das, North 24 Parganas

editorials.title: Stolen shine
editorials.passage:
Two young Chinese academics have won this year’s prestigious Fields Medal, awarded to mathematicians under 40. The only thing is, they don’t work in China. The awards have, of course, been celebrated as a national achievement. But they have also sparked off intense debate over whether the achievement has anything to do with the academics’ alma mater , Peking University. The university was quick to claim them as its own, displaying their names in neon lights on a campus pagoda.

The discussion is reminiscent of Indian reactions to the achievements of Indians who make their mark overseas. But in her acceptance speech, Hong Wang, the 35-year-old who is now only the third woman to win this award in its 90-year history, did not even mention Peking University in her acceptance message. Worse, in an interview, she said she had felt discouraged as an undergraduate at the university. Her remarks created a furore.

Some Chinese thanked her for speaking out against the feelings of inadequacy and pessimism that had dogged them through university. Others highlighted how even a second prize is celebrated in Europe but frowned upon as not good enough by Chinese parents. A post on social media by a PhD student who was waiting for his supervisor’s signature to complete his thesis went viral as an affirmation of Hong’s experience. After repeated pleadings, the supervisor’s final reply to him was: “You’re like an ant to me.”

Hong, the daughter of middle school teachers in the city of Guilin, was solving complex maths problems at the age of six. Despite her talent and determination, she failed to secure the only seat reserved by Peking University’s mathematics department for students from her province, Guangxi, and had to enrol in another department. There, she took maths minors and studied maths courses on her own, and eventually managed to get a transfer to the department that she always wanted to join.

However, she soon began to feel that she was not good enough and doubted whether she would qualify for a postgraduate seat at the university. Unsure whether she was even cut out for maths, she took a chance when France’s renowned École Polytechnique came recruiting. She passed their entrance exam and went off to France to study architecture. But soon, encouraged by the teachers around her, she went back to her first love. It was her French teachers whom she thanked the most in her acceptance speech.

In the meantime, her interview led to caustic comments about her abilities: after all, critics argued, she hadn’t exactly shone in her country’s most prestigious university.

Deng Yu, the other Fields medallist, now 37, had spent just two years as an undergraduate at Peking University before going off to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to complete his education. An interview he’d given before winning the medal was carried in full by Peking University’s School of Mathematical Sciences’ social media handle, but the version posted on the university’s main handle was edited. The portions deleted related to his views on studying abroad and returning to China.

Chinese students should spend at least one substantial stint of their academic career overseas to broaden their horizons by experiencing a different academic system and engaging with new colleagues, was Deng’s advice. While deciding to return, they should evaluate which environment best suits their research, lifestyle, and long-term plans.

Why was such reasonable advice censored? Perhaps Peking University didn’t want to fuel the popular resentment towards Chinese students abroad. Those who don’t return are blamed for brain drain; those who do are criticised for taking advantage of China’s welcoming measures for scholars forced back home by the current adverse academic atmosphere in the US. Either way, they fail the test of patriotism.

editorials.title: Grim fate: Editorial on climate crisis and the growing threat to humanity
editorials.passage:
The future of the planet is bleak: the findings of fresh reports from the United Nations have confirmed the possibility. Limiting Overshoot Spotlight Report , compiled by the UNEP, has projected that an indifferent world is on its way to breaching the 1.5 degree Celsius barrier — the red flag of the Paris Agreement of 2015. Even if every nation were to honour its pledge of meeting its climate goals — a rather optimistic assumption — global temperatures are expected to rise by around 2.6 degree Celsius by 2100 above pre-industrial levels. The outcome, quite naturally, would be catastrophic. More bad news comes from the World Meteorological Organization, which says that a “supersized” El Nino could compound the rising heat on land and in oceans on account of climate change. Worse, the phenomenon is expected to last till early next year, raising the prospects of drought, steep disruptions in global trade and economy as well as monumental damage to ecological systems. And that is not the end of the dire tidings. Rising oceans are threatening coastal habitations all over the world — Mumbai and Calcutta are particularly at risk. Sea levels rose by 4.7mm annually between 2014 and 2023; the figure for 2024 was 5.9mm. High income economies stand to lose assets worth 2-3.5 trillion dollars while poor and middle income nations are expected to shoulder an unprecedented crisis in the form of human displacement.

The most likely — human — response to the scale of the environmental crisis would be immobility and inertia. Yet, these are exactly the responses that the global fraternity needs to avoid. There is no time to lose given the existential nature of the crisis. Hope, too, is slimming — but it has not been extinguished completely. For instance, one of the UN reports has unveiled that the world can still strive and lower the rising temperatures even after they have breached the 1.5 degree Celsius mark: an undesirable means but possibly the only option left now. For this to happen, countries can no longer rely on their political representatives. Years of failed climate negotiations by inept, uncaring and corrupt politicians has brought Armageddon nigh. Instead, the only recourse ought to be interventions — sustained protests, public sensitisation, debates, informed electoral choices and so on — by people’s collectives the world over. A silver lining is the fledgling demand for accountability on ecological concerns from politicians by young voters, especially in the first world. This heartening culture needs to spread. Policy and people must unite to avoid environmental doomsday.

editorials.title: Right to ask: Editorial on shrinking space for dissent in India
editorials.passage:
At a time when questioning is discouraged and dissent punished, the remarks of the Supreme Court judge, Ujjal Bhuyan, were heartening. Speaking at the convocation ceremony of the National Law University, Delhi, the judge said that the right to question is not an act of defiance. He not only presented questioning as a right in a democracy but also said that it was an expression of citizenship, liberty and constitutional responsibility. A democracy is participatory, according to the vision the judge projected; hence questioning was an outcome of the freedom of expression as well as responsible citizenship. These issues have become contentious: proofs of citizenship are confusing and the freedom to express divergent opinions is stifled. The judge’s remarks also touched on intolerance, stating that the constitutional framework of free expression, thinking and believing differently was undermined when disagreement was rejected, silenced or punished. From the speech, the citizen could be seen as the heart of a democracy; his or her questions and criticisms would be part of the spectrum of thinking out of which the character of the democracy was moulded. Mr Bhuyan felt that instead of treating each dissent as a threat, the government should listen to citizens and give space to their opinion. The maturity of a democracy was displayed in the way it responded to difficult or inconvenient opinions, not merely to popular ones blessed by majoritarian mandate.

What was perhaps especially important in the speech was the importance he gave to universities. Universities throughout India — as in West Bengal — have been and are being targeted as bastions of ‘anti-national’ thinking. This is an attack on intellectual freedom and the search of young people for their place in society, a society to which they wish to contribute. Mr Bhuyan said that a democratic culture which respects liberty and difference is born in the university where the habit of thinking freely begins. Here, students do not hesitate to ask questions because the answer may be uncomfortable. The judge’s remarks seemed to bring out the reason why universities are unpopular with the government today. His emphasis on the space for dissent, for divergent opinions, is of overwhelming importance. For him, the essence of a liberal constitutional democracy is the ability to live with disagreement. How far does today’s India uphold this ideal?

editorials.title: A battle over the soul of IBC’s Part III norms
editorials.passage:
National Company Law Tribunal benches are not enlarged lightly, but because the institution itself recognises that the questions before it deserve an answer that will outlive the immediate dispute. The proceedings concerning Subhash Chandra have travelled from a split Bench to a third member and now to a five-member Bench, which has stayed the implementation of the repayment plan.

The immediate dispute concerns the repayment plan of a personal guarantor (PG). The larger debate concerns the interpretation of Part III of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), the framework governing insolvency of individuals and personal guarantors. Should an economic statute be interpreted by reference to its words alone, or also by the commercial purpose which Parliament intended it to serve? This dichotomy lies at the heart of the present reference.

Nearly 50 years ago, Justice VR Krishna Iyer observed in Kanta Goel v. B.P. Pathak that “the legislative project and purpose turn not on niceties of little verbalism but on the actualities of rugged realism” and that the statutory construction must be “illumined by the goal, though guided by the word.” That insight is as relevant today as it was in 1977. Every economic statute influences behaviour in the marketplace, and its words must be read in the light of the purpose Parliament intended them to serve.

The difference between the judicial member and the technical member reflected two different conceptions of the level of scrutiny expected from a Resolution Professional (RP) and, ultimately, from the Adjudicating Authority itself. The third member sought a middle course. Whether that course fully answers the concerns raised by the technical member is what now falls for consideration before the larger Bench.

The judicial member confined himself to the statutory text: if the claims admitted by the RP satisfied the statutory framework and the requisite majority, the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority was necessarily limited.

The technical member’s concern went to the integrity of the creditor constituency itself. Her opinion raises a series of questions concerning asset tracing, forensic scrutiny, the admission of guarantees in favour of allegedly connected entities and the acceptance of claims on behalf of more than 1,200 individuals without independent verification.

The Code recognises the wife of the PG’s brother as an ‘associate’ for the purposes of the Code. On the judicial member’s construction, a company controlled by that very associate would escape scrutiny merely because the PG himself held no shares in it. The technical member felt that section 79(2)(g) required a purposive construction that recognised not only direct ownership, but also the aggregate ownership and control exercised through associates.

She reasoned that the nature of the purported guarantees was extortionate, stipulating interest at 12 per cent per annum from invocation. This led her to question whether these entities ought to have been treated as independent creditors without a more searching enquiry, an approach consistent with the principle recognised by the Supreme Court in Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. v. Spade Finance Services Ltd.

The third member’s opinion is no manifesto for literalism. Instead, it repeatedly reaffirms the supervisory role of the Adjudicating Authority, recognises that commercial wisdom cannot override statutory requirements and cautions against converting the RP into a forensic investigator and the insolvency process into an open-ended enquiry. Insolvency proceedings cannot become hostage to speculative allegations or endless investigations. That approach has much to commend it.

But the technical member’s concerns do not altogether disappear. While the third member repeatedly asks whether there is convincing material establishing concealment, suppression or statutory non-compliance, the technical member asks at what point objectively verifiable circumstances require the RP to ask more searching questions. That enquiry precedes any finding of fraud or wrongdoing. It concerns the standard of professional scrutiny which the Code expects of an RP.

That brings one to the real difficulty. The absence of conclusive evidence regarding the role of the associates, the nature of their guarantees and their entitlement to sit on the creditors’ Committee leads once to ask whether the objective circumstances before the RP required him to investigate the matter further.

As regards net worth, the PG disclosed a personal net worth of about ₹31.79 crore. But statements furnished to RBL Bank in 2017 and Canara Bank in 2018 reflected approximately $7.17 billion and ₹40,562 crore respectively. The PG’s explanation that the earlier statements reflected investments held through promoter group companies rather than assets personally owned by him does not, by itself, answer the concern. If that financial strength formed part of the representation upon which substantial credit was obtained, why does it become wholly irrelevant under Part III?

The guarantees illustrate the same point. They form part of the objective commercial relationship between the PG and the entities in whose favour substantial liabilities were voluntarily assumed. Therein lies the technical member’s central point. Rule 4 of the PG Rules and the Explanation to section 5(24A) read with section 79(2)(g) recognise certain familial relationships and exclude their vote from the creditors committee. In her view, private familial arrangements cannot efface statutorily recognised relationships. If the PG’s brother’s wife is herself an associate, can a company overwhelmingly controlled by her escape statutory consequence merely because the PG holds no shares in it? The technical member felt that such a construction would permit the very mischief which section 109(4)(b) was enacted to prevent.

One further aspect deserved more direct engagement. The procedural chronology raises a similar concern. The RP filed his report the day after the repayment plan was submitted. Creditors were given six days before the meeting, though section 106(4)(a) prescribes a minimum of 14 days. The RP cited a resolution reducing the notice period. The technical member held that a resolution could not override a statutory requirement. The third member ruled that it was not fatal. The question is whether a creditors’ resolution can override a mandatory statutory requirement. If Parliament prescribed a minimum period for creditor deliberation, that safeguard could not be displaced.

Interestingly, the third member did not regard the process as entirely beyond criticism. He agreed that the claims of Anil Kumar and Sunil Jain, representing over 1,200 individuals, could not be admitted merely on the strength of the PG’s explanation, and directed their exclusion. That raises a larger question: if the RP’s duty of verification required exclusion of claims constituting 0.8 per cent voting share, why did the same duty not warrant closer scrutiny of claims accounting for more than 60 per cent, where ‘associateship’ objections had been raised?

Every insolvency process rests upon confidence in the integrity of the steps that precede the final order. Notices, verification of claims and statutory safeguards are not procedural formalities; they are the means by which confidence in the outcome is earned. The five-member Bench has before it an opportunity to define the standard of vigilance which Part III expects before commercial wisdom is permitted to prevail. That standard will shape lender confidence, professional conduct and, ultimately, the credibility of the personal insolvency framework itself.

The writer is a lawyer and former Judicial Member of the National Company Law Tribunal

editorials.title: Women’s empowerment — schools and beyond
editorials.passage:
The National Family Health Survey (2023-24) Fact Sheets evoke reflection. Read with the five earlier Surveys starting from 1992-93, they reflect a tale of transformation and persistent challenges as well. We decided to look at the findings from the lens of gender empowerment, which encompasses opportunities for vibrant women’s collectives, access to quality education, having a voice and agency to take decisions, access to economic activity and diversified livelihoods.

The last decade and a half have seen rural livelihood mission collectives expand to a 100 million women. While studies indicate persistence of patriarchy in modified forms, it is also true that a lot has changed in the lives of women on account of the collectives. Access to credit, low wage employment and low profit nano enterprises, access to animal resources, adolescent girls in secondary education, women in farm and non-farm livelihoods, better access to reproductive and child health, clean water and sanitation, cash transfers, free travel in some States, are all making a difference to the lives of women. Interestingly, the rural livelihood mission has managed to capture the imagination of all political parties who are vying with each other to do more for women as they are the largest constituency.

We decided to look at NFHS-6 Fact Sheets across States on indicators like 6+ females ever attended school, 2-4 years in pre-school, 10 years of schooling for 15-49-year-old males and females and stunting among under 5-year-old children. These were purposively selected as they reveal a lot on the role that these indicators play in the lives of women and development. To understand the inter-State variations better, we looked at the better (Sikkim, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Goa, Himachal Pradesh), the aspiring (Bihar, UP, MP, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh) and a few high on per capita income States but without commensurate social development indicators (Haryana, Gujarat, Telangana, Maharashtra and Karnataka) to understand how gender empowerment matters to real development.

As is well known, 69.23 per cent of 6+ rural females had never been enrolled in primary education at the time of the 42nd Round National Sample Survey (1986-87). With 73.7 per cent of 6+ females ever attended school in 2023-24, surely a lot has changed; Kerala reports 96.6 per cent. Bihar and Rajasthan have not been able to shed this historical disadvantage in girls’ education as they are at 64 per cent. Surprisingly, in Telangana, only 60.2 per cent of the 6+ females have ever attended school. Despite high per capita income, the State has major challenges in girls’ education.

The data on men and women with 10 or more years of schooling among the 15-49 population is equally insightful. Kerala tops with 86.6 per cent females against 82.1 per cent males. Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat are below 40 per cent on this indicator. Telangana reports a 13.9 per cent gender gap on the indicators for 10 years of schooling, pointing out how it needs to do much more to bridge the gender gap. Haryana, even though very high on per capita income, reports a high 9.2 per cent gender gap on 10 years of schooling. Clearly, gender unequal relationships are a cause of concern to development and well-being.

Gender inequalities in States reflect strongly in the level of stunting among children under age five. As is to be expected, the States in the better category are all below the national average of stunting at 29.3 per cent, the aspiring States are all above the national average, but the surprising performance is some of the States like Haryana, Telangana, Gujarat, and to some extent even Maharashtra and Karnataka, where the figures are sobering in comparison to their economic performance. These States must reduce the gender gap in 10 years of schooling to make a dent on stunting among children, as a correlation has been observed. Women’s education, empowerment, voice, agency and collectives make a difference to gender gaps over time, and we need to invest in such processes. It is also true that some regions in these States have special challenges.

States like Sikkim, Meghalaya, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar have made significant progress in reducing stunting in recent years through collaborative governance using women’s collectives. The Panchayati Raj Institutions-Self-Help Group (PRI-SHG) framework has facilitated a more gender sensitive approach to development.

The less than 50 per cent coverage of 2-4-year-olds in pre-school shows that the Integrated Child Development Services scheme is still far from achieving universal coverage. It is higher than the national average in the better States, indicating the important role that pre-school education plays in the holistic development of a child. It is for this reason that the new National Education Policy 2020 has rightly emphasised the importance of pre-school education.

To fulfil the aspiration of the National Education Policy, a lot more will need to be done. The army of women caregivers like Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Aanganwadi workers and helpers have all played a key role in meeting the needs of the 0-6-year-old children.

However, low compensation to these women workers at the last mile, compromises our ability to provide high-quality day-care centres and crèches for children of working women. This has implications for female labour force participation rates. We need to revisit the governance and compensation framework of the last mile, locally resident women workers, to ensure high-quality care services that are needed for quality human capital, productivity and economic growth.

The NFHS-6 also highlights better performance of States that have invested in devolution, decentralised community action. PRI-SHG partnerships, girls’ education, and an overall framework of collaborative governance and gender empowerment. Women’s collectives, voice, agency and empowerment is the pathway to inclusive growth and well-being. That is the lesson from the NFHS-6 data.

editorials.title: An apple, an orange and 2.6 per cent
editorials.passage:
There are three kinds of lies. Lies, damned lies and statistics. Twain said Disraeli said it. The records suggest Disraeli never did. Even the quote has a revision problem. The attribution was updated as evidence improved. India’s Q1 GDP now enjoys similar treatment. The official estimate is 7.8 per cent real growth. Nominal growth is 10.3 per cent. A rival figure claims 2.6 per cent. That figure deserves dissection. Not as economics. As entertainment. The recipe is simple. Take this year’s Q1, ₹88.27 lakh crore. That sits on the new 2022-23 base. Divide by last year’s ₹86.05 lakh crore. That sat on the old 2011-12 base. Different base, different methods, different coverage. This is dividing an apple by an orange. The quotient is fruit salad. Serve chilled, on prime time.

The paper trail is public and dull. On August 29, 2025, Q1 FY26 was ₹86.05 lakh crore. February 2026 brought the new series. The figure became ₹80.32 lakh crore. June 2026 made it ₹80.44 lakh crore. New IIP and PPI series then arrived. It settled at ₹80 lakh crore. Four steps. Each dated. Each published. As heists go, this one issued press releases.

Now do the sum properly. ₹88.27 over ₹80.32 gives 10.3 per cent. Distrust February? Use the June vintage instead. Nominal growth is still 9.7 per cent. Real growth is about 7.4 per cent. Not 2.6. You cannot reach 2.6 without mixing the fruit. Statistics has one iron rule. Compare like with like. Cricket averages are not computed across formats. A Test average is not divided by T20 innings. Nobody races this year’s marathon against last year’s sprint. GDP deserves the same courtesy. It rarely receives it in August.

Why rebase at all? Ask the IMF. Its 2025 data adequacy assessment graded our national accounts C. Like a strict schoolmaster, it listed the faults. A base year stuck in 2011-12. Single deflation with WPI, for want of a PPI. Unexplained discrepancies between production and expenditure. The February 2026 rebasing fixed exactly these. A 2022-23 base, double deflation, a proper PPI. The IMF called it critical and welcome. The homework the examiner demanded is now called cheating.

Could we have rebased earlier? Base years must be boring years. 2016-17 had demonetisation. 2017-18 had the GST transition. Then Covid ate two more. 2022-23 was the first year that behaved. Base years are like passport photographs. Choose a calm day. Statisticians waited for the economy to sit still. Photographers with toddlers will understand.

Now grade the alleged conspiracy. Last year was supposedly shrunk to flatter this year. Three difficulties arise. First, the shrinking was announced six months in advance. Conspiracies rarely come with a press calendar. Second, the rebasing cut nominal GDP by 4 per cent. Cooks who shrink their own kitchen are rare. Third, MoSPI released 64 tables of methodology. No self-respecting fudger loves annexures this much.

Here is the delicious part. The 7.8 is provisional. It will be revised until February 2029. On the old base, FY22 to FY25 saw 25 upward revisions. Downward ones numbered 12. The odds favour up, not down. Today’s 7.8 could plausibly become 8.2. Will the critics then apologise? At current prices or constant? History suggests neither. Revisions travel both ways. Outrage travels only one.

Nor is revision an Indian vice. The US Bureau of Economic Analysis revises perpetually. Its 2024 study covers 1999 to 2022. Advance estimates moved 1.2 percentage points on average. Comprehensive revisions arrive every five years. The UK revises. Japan revises. Everyone revises. Only astrologers never do. Timeliness has a price. That price is called revision. Only the final number is final. And even that gets a comprehensive haircut.

Meanwhile, some numbers cannot be conjured. GST till August was ₹10.42 lakh crore, up 11 per cent. Passenger vehicles rose 25.6 per cent. August dispatches grew 35 per cent. Commercial vehicles grew over 40 per cent. Tractors rose 19 per cent, cement 8.8 per cent. Exports till July grew 17 per cent. Net FDI rose from $4.75 billion to $7.8 billion. An economy limping at 2.6 does not buy tractors like this. Cement does not read press releases. Tractors have no politics. Taxes, unlike television arguments, are paid in cash.

A final tutorial, free of charge. The 2.6 is a current price number. Growth is compared at constant prices. Current prices carry inflation inside them. Undergraduates learn this in week one. Some forget it between the green room and the camera.

None of this canonises 7.8. Doubt is a public service. Real wages remain soft. Good jobs remain a fair question. Ask those questions, and loudly. But ask them on one series. Otherwise it is not scrutiny. It is theatre with a calculator.

A party meme showed the economy as beer and the data as froth. Good image, wrong glass. The froth is in the 2.6. The beer is real. And come 2029, it may well pour taller.

editorials.title: US’ mid-term anxieties
editorials.passage:
There used to be times in America when almost any perceived controversial policy was pegged as a diversion from the Epstein files, the bulky dossier of the wealthy and disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein who hobnobbed with political elites and later spent time in jail for crimes including for trafficking in women especially minor girls. He died while in prison, his death officially ruled as suicide. US President Donald Trump was known to Epstein but not a shred of evidence of any wrongdoing.

Fortunately for Trump and the Republicans in a Congressional Mid Term elections time few are talking about the Epstein files per se or as a diversionary mechanism. It has shifted gears to renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America after the recent tiff between Washington and Ottawa. That was the last thing that the Grand Old Party especially its members in the House of Representatives and Senate seeking re-election needed, particularly those whose districts border with Canada.

In fact it is said that some Republicans are alarmed that the recent Canada tariffs could hurt efforts in holding on to the Senate especially in the competitive races in states like Alaska, Maine, Michigan and Ohio. The tariff war unleashed means that Americans would have to fork out extra money, especially at a time when they are already complaining of high grocery bills and prices at pumps. No wonder then that the name change to Lake America fell flat: Americans opposed the Executive Order 63 per cent to 14 per cent, the rest undecided. Even Republicans too disagreed by 43 per cent to 33 per cent margin. Another assessment is that Americans are not blaming Canadians for the escalation with 46 per cent in a poll hold the US responsible for the dispute.

What worries the Republican leadership barely two months to go for the November 3 showdown is that Trump’s approval rating is stuck at 33 per cent, the lowest level of his time in office. A Reuters/Ipsos poll shows a President dragged down by the war in Iran and the economic leadership with 71 per cent disapproving of his handling of the cost of living problem.

Of more serious concern to the GOP is that the poll shows 46 per cent of Democrats are very enthusiastic about voting in November as opposed to 31 per cent of Republicans; and among Independents, 36 per cent would vote Democratic and 22 per cent Republican.

What must really hit the Republican Party hard is Trump’s 14-point drop in approval rating, from 47 per cent in the early second term to 33 per cent now. And hurting more will be another statistic — that Trump is lower than where his predecessor Democratic President Joe Biden was in October 2024 at 35 per cent. The Iran war has an approval of a mere 36 per cent. It is also pointed out that registered voters in the latest survey have taken the view that the Democratic Party has better ideas for the economy than the Republicans, a first time lead for Democrats apparently in about a decade.

What has also attracted attention in political circles is a private meeting between Trump’s son-in-law and confidante Jared Kushner and Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the discussion apparently touching on issues of cost of living, housing and immigration. Whether the meeting is in anticipation of Democrats getting hold of the House is a matter of speculation; but the discussion has caused indignation among Democratic Left wing and Progressives who want an aggressive evaluation of the administration with some talk of even a third Impeachment of Trump in the House should power change hands.

What is unfolding in an election scene is a sense of apprehension among both Republicans and Democrats, but for different reasons: the GOP’s anxious to hold on; and the Democrats anxious to hold together in the event of a win. The recent defection of two Democrats in a House Rules vote is seen as an indication of things to come.

The writer is a senior journalist who has reported from Washington DC on North America and United Nations

editorials.title: Beyond the 7.8% number
editorials.passage: By Saumitra Bhaduri & KR Shanmugam, Respectively Professor and former Director, Madras School of Economics The first-quarter GDP data released earlier this week, which widely beat forecasts, has sparked a fresh controversy over its credibility. Real GDP growth accelerated to 7.8% in Q1 of FY27, well above the RBI’s 7% estimate, reinforcing the impression of a resilient economy despite a difficult global environment. However, the controversy over India’s GDP numbers is not new. It has been around since the introduction of the new GDP series, with questions over the old and new base years, revisions to historical estimates, and, more recently, changes in the data and methodology used to measure output. Therefore, before questioning whether the latest GDP number is credible, it may be wise to establish exactly what the problem is. The first fact is straightforward. India has changed its GDP series. In February, the ministry of statistics and programme implementation replaced the 2011-12 base-year series with one using 2022-23 as the base year. This is not simply a change in the reference year. The new series incorporates new data sources, changes in coverage and classification, improved deflators, and a new method for benchmarking quarterly estimates. That matters because the new series has substantially changed the measured size of the economy. Consider Q1 of FY26. Under the old 2011-12 series, nominal GDP was estimated at Rs 86.05 lakh crore. Under the new 2022-23 series, the estimate for the same quarter is Rs 80 lakh crore. The ministry has, however, defended the revision as reflecting the use of new price and production indices with base year 2022-23. ALSO READRethinking the way we work Now consider Q1 of FY27. Nominal GDP under the new series is Rs 88.27 lakh crore, compared with Rs 80 lakh crore a year earlier. That gives nominal GDP growth of 10.3%. The reported 7.8% growth rate is based on constant-price GDP. Under the new series, real GDP in Q1 of FY26 was Rs 75.46 lakh crore, while Q1 of FY27 is estimated at Rs 81.36 lakh crore. The increase between the two is 7.8%. This is where the controversy begins. As some incorrectly argue, if one takes the old estimate of Rs 86.05 lakh crore for Q1 of FY26 and uses it as the denominator against the new Rs 88.27 lakh crore estimate for Q1 of FY27, the increase is only 2.6%, and they question whether the reported growth rate is being inflated by the change in the GDP series. Therefore, those arguing that the 7.8% growth rate is actually 2.6% are mixing two different things. The 2.6% calculation is based on nominal GDP, while the 7.8% figure refers to real GDP growth. More importantly, the two nominal GDP numbers being compared come from different series. To resolve the controversy fairly, we need an estimate of Q1 FY27 constructed using the old methodology. Unfortunately, that number no longer exists as an official estimate. However, since an appropriate old-versus-new comparison is not possible, the question then becomes whether other economic indicators corroborate the broad growth story. These indicators cannot prove that GDP grew by 7.8%, but they can tell us whether the underlying direction of economic activity is consistent with a strong first quarter. Several indicators are useful for this purpose. The most important are industrial production, capital formation, private final consumption expenditure, bank credit, exports, corporate performance, and GST collections. Industrial production grew by 6.7% in July, compared to 5.4% last year. It increased by 6.3% in April-July FY27, compared to 4.0% in the same period last year. Capital goods production rose by 16.1% this July over July 2025. Intermediate goods increased by10.0% and infrastructure and construction goods by 6.9%. ALSO READThe city is losing its soundtrack The investment story, for one, is encouraging. Gross fixed capital formation grew 11.9% in Q1 FY27, compared with 5.8% a year earlier. Private final consumption expenditure (PFCE) also registered healthy growth of 7.1% compared with the corresponding period last year (6.8%). Bank credit provides another corroborative signal. Credit to industry grew 20% in July, compared with 6.5% a year earlier, while credit to services expanded 22.9% against 10.2% previously. Agricultural credit also accelerated to 17% from 7.3%. Such broad-based credit expansion suggests the increase in economic activity is not confined to government spending or a few sectors. Exports also strengthened. Real exports grew 12% in Q1, compared with 6% a year earlier. More recent data show that combined merchandise and services exports reached an estimated $80.14 billion in July, up 13.3% from a year earlier. Cumulative exports during April-July were $316.42 billion. Corporate activity offers a similar, though somewhat mixed, picture. Private-sector sales accelerated sharply in Q1, while corporate investment also appears to be recovering. RBI data show private corporate sector sales rising 19.4% year-on-year (y-o-y) in Q1 FY27, although higher input costs and taxes meant that the improvement in profits was much less pronounced. GST collections provide another broad indicator of activity. Gross GST collections rose 15.4% y-o-y to Rs 2.11 lakh crore in July, while domestic GST collections increased 10.1%. In August, gross collections were close to Rs 2 lakh crore, up 14.8% from a year earlier. Cumulatively, gross GST collections during April-August were up about 11%. These numbers are consistent with reasonably strong domestic economic activity, although GST collections are also influenced by compliance and import values. Taken together, these indicators make it difficult to argue that the 7.8% GDP number has no economic foundation. Index of industrial production, investment, credit, exports, corporate sales, and tax collections are all pointing broadly in the same direction. While they do not statistically validate the GDP estimate, they corroborate the underlying momentum. Yet there are reasons for caution. Employment remains one of them. The latest PLFS data are encouraging on the surface: the unemployment rate fell to 5.1% in July from 5.5% in June, while the labour force participation rate rose to 55.4% and the worker population ratio to 52.5%. But these numbers do not tell us enough about the quality, productivity, or remuneration of the jobs being created. A high-growth economy ultimately needs to translate output growth into productive and better-paying employment. Foreign investment is another area to watch. Gross FDI flows to India increased 14.8% in April-June FY27, while net FDI rose to $7.9 billion from $4.8 billion a year earlier. This is positive, but net outward FDI was also $9.3 billion. Most importantly, risks largely unrelated to the statistical debate could materially affect the growth outlook. Oil prices have become a concern again. Brent crude was around $95 a barrel on September 3, amid renewed US-Iran tensions and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. For an economy heavily dependent on imported crude, a prolonged oil shock can widen the trade deficit, raise inflation, and squeeze domestic demand. The monsoon presents another uncertainty. August rainfall was 16% below normal, taking cumulative rainfall for June-August to about 86% of the long-period average. The IMD expects September rainfall to be below normal as well. This creates risks for kharif yields, rural incomes, and, consequently, rural consumption in the second half of the year. The 7.8% growth number should therefore be neither dismissed as fabricated nor accepted without scrutiny. Credibility ultimately depends on transparency around a consistent back series, a clear old-to-new reconciliation, and enough disclosure for independent researchers to reproduce the estimates, which could finally put the controversy at rest.

editorials.title: RBI accounting deprives govt of full surplus
editorials.passage: The RBI announced a surplus transfer of Rs 2,86,588 crore to the government for FY26, 6.7% more than the Rs 2,68,590 crore in FY25. Yet its accounts suggest that significant realised earnings continue to be retained in reserves. Between FY22 and FY26, Rs 4,42,504 crore was transferred to the Contingency Fund (CF). The FY26 allocation alone rose sharply to Rs 1,09,380 crore from Rs 44,862 crore in FY25. Although foreign-exchange income is volatile and can affect annual surpluses, the RBI’s accounting framework still appears to retain capital beyond its own prescribed requirements. In FY26, it reported interest income of Rs 2,35,580 crore, including Rs 1,35,215 crore from foreign sources. Foreign-source “other income” was Rs 1,92,440 crore, comprising exchange gains of Rs 1,68,906 crore, amortisation of premium or discount of Rs 16,354 crore, profit on foreign-security sales of Rs 3,503 crore, and miscellaneous income of Rs 3,676 crore. The RBI reported a 6.4% yield on average foreign currency assets (FCA), up from 5.3% in FY25, reflecting comprehensive returns including trading gains. ALSO READBeyond the 7.8% number Foreign securities (FS) and rupee securities (RS) are marked to market daily, with unrealised gains and losses recorded in investment revaluation accounts (IRA-FS and IRA-RS). At the end of FY26, IRA-FS had a debit balance of Rs 90,833 crore, against Rs 81,367 crore in FY25. IRA-RS moved from a Rs 16,843 crore credit to a Rs 30,604 crore debit as domestic yields hardened. The Foreign Exchange Forward Contracts Valuation Account (FCVA) similarly moved from a Rs 6,985 crore credit to a Rs 43,403 crore debit, matched by a contra provision under “other liabilities”. These three debit balances are charged to the CF at the year-end and reversed on the next financial year’s first working day. Meanwhile, unrealised rupee gains and losses on FCA and gold arising from exchange-rate and gold-price movements bypass the income statement and flow into the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA). Rupee depreciation and higher gold prices lifted the CGRA from Rs 13,02,965 crore in FY25 to Rs 21,68,530 crore in FY26. The CGRA covers foreign-currency assets and gold, but no equivalent account exists for rupee securities. The resulting structure is asymmetric. Changes in the market value of FS and RS pass through separate IRA accounts, while the increase in the rupee value of FCA and gold is accumulated in the CGRA. None enters income unless realised. Yet debit balances in IRA-FS, IRA-RS, and FCVA reduce the CF at each year-end, even though the foreign-asset revaluation gains held in the CGRA remain outside realised equity. This separation obscures both the underlying risk position and the surplus available for distribution. ALSO READRethinking the way we work The Bimal Jalan Committee recommended maintaining the CF at 5.5-6.5% of balance-sheet assets (BSA). Under the revised Economic Capital Framework approved on May 15, 2025, the Contingent Risk Buffer, which subsumes the CF, may range from 4.5% to 7.5% of BSA. For FY26, the RBI’s Central Board chose 6.5%, below the 7.5% applied in FY25. Available realised equity (ARE), comprising capital, the reserve fund, CF, and asset development fund, stood at Rs 5,97,813 crore, or 6.5% of BSA (Rs 91,97,121 crore). Total economic capital, including revaluation accounts, was Rs 27,66,343 crore, or 30.08% of BSA, above the committee’s recommended 20.8-25.4% range. However, this capital is measured against assets at their rupee mark-to-market value, while risk crystallises against their historic rupee cost only after revaluation balances are exhausted. Deducting total revaluation accounts of Rs 21,68,530 crore produces BSA at a cost of Rs 70,28,591 crore. Against this base, economic capital rises to 39.36%, while ARE equals 8.505%. For FY25, the adjustment raises economic capital to 30.14% of BSA net of revaluation accounts. The FY26 increase shows how unrealised currency and gold gains can distort reported capital ratios. It implies excess realised equity even against the revised framework’s 7.5% ceiling. Using unrounded figures, the excess is roughly 1.005% of Rs 70,28,591 crore, or Rs 70,669 crore, which could have been distributed to the government. Against the 6.5% buffer actually selected for FY26, the additional retention rises to roughly Rs 1,40,954 crore. The RBI should calculate its contingency buffer and economic capital against BSA net of revaluation accounts. It should also consolidate cross-border revaluations: IRA-FS and FCVA balances should be adjusted against the CGRA, which captures changes in the rupee value of overseas assets, rather than charged to the CF. The CF could then be maintained at a transparent, conservatively higher ratio, such as 10% of net BSA, funded solely through allocations from realised surplus. Adding back the FY26 IRA-FS debit of Rs 90,833 crore and FCVA debit of Rs 43,403 crore would take the CF to Rs 7,02,569 crore, exactly 10% of net BSA. The Rs 30,604 crore IRA-RS debit should not be added back because rupee securities lack a corresponding revaluation reserve. Revaluation accounts would consequently decline to Rs 20,34,294 crore. Four reforms follow. First, set off IRA-FS and FCVA against the CGRA at year-end, allowing rupee appreciation or depreciation to change the CGRA transparently. Second, allocate realised surplus to the CF when required, without IRA adjustments. Third, calculate both the CF and economic capital on BSA net of revaluation accounts, using a higher ratio if prudence demands. Fourth, exclude zero- or negligible-default-risk assets from the contingency base. Loans and advances to banks and governments, reverse repos, and accrued income total `5,60,599 crore; applying a 6.5% reserve to them retains an additional Rs 36,439 crore. The RBI is wholly owned by the government of India, which can recapitalise it if necessary. Its balance-sheet risks ultimately belong to the sovereign, and its economic capital is, in substance, government equity. Excess capital retained by the RBI reduces government revenue, forcing additional borrowing and a higher fiscal deficit to finance expenditure. It must therefore simplify its accounting, improve disclosure, and apply the high transparency standards it requires of regulated entities. A clearer framework would preserve robust central-bank risk capital while ensuring that the government receives its legitimate share of realised surplus.
